British Policy to the Declaration

Header: The Boston Massacre, engraving by Paul Revere, 1770. Cover: Declaration of Independence, painting by John Trumbull, 1819. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.
Mini-lesson · Mr. Peregrin

From Quarrel to Declaration

Today's Focus

Why did colonists who loved the British Crown decide to leave it?

For more than a hundred years, the colonists governed themselves in many ways. Then Britain tried to change that. This lesson follows the policies one by one and asks which right each one touched.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to…
  1. describe the main British policies from 1763 to 1775 and the colonial response
  2. explain why reconciliation was still possible until the king rejected the Olive Branch Petition
  3. match grievances in the Declaration to the natural rights it says were violated
Quick Check-in

Before you read: when is it right for a people to break away from their government? Make your best guess.

Try it, then check
In your notebook, write why Parliament thought the colonists should help pay after the French and Indian War. Then show the answer to compare.
The war had nearly doubled Britain’s debt. Parliament decided that the colonists, who had been defended, should help pay.
Decide
There is no wrong answer. Make a choice, then see what colonists did.
The year is 1765. Parliament has passed the Stamp Act, which taxes printed papers of every kind, even playing cards. The colonists have no members in Parliament. What would you do first?
This was the colonists’ main argument. “No taxation without representation” became their cry.
Merchants did this. They boycotted British goods.
Crowds in the streets did frighten the tax collectors.
What actually happened. Colonists did all three. The protest worked, and in 1766 Parliament repealed the Stamp Act. But on the same day it passed the Declaratory Act, which said that Parliament could make laws for the colonies in all cases.
Put it in order
Tap these seven events in the order they happened.
Flip the cards
Think of the meaning first, then tap each card to check.
Follow the argument
Tap Next to follow how the Declaration builds its case.
Step one: the principles
The opening paragraphs say that all men are created equal and have rights from their Creator. Governments exist to secure those rights, and they rest on the consent of the governed.
Step two: the right to change
When a government becomes destructive of these ends, the people may alter or abolish it. But governments long established should not be changed for light and transient causes.
Step three: the charges
The Declaration then lists many grievances against King George. It argues that the colonists have suffered a long train of abuses.
Step four: the proof
If the charges are true, then Locke’s right of revolution applies. The rest of the document is the proof for the opening paragraphs.
Step five: the reader decides
The Declaration asks “a candid world” to judge. A good citizen asks of each charge whether it is true and whether it is serious enough for so grave a step.

Your Answer Now

Why did colonists who loved the British Crown decide to leave it? Answer in three or four sentences, using at least two details from the book.

The Big Question

When may a free people change its government, and how should a good citizen judge whether the cause is serious enough?

Write your answer in four or five sentences. Use at least two things you have learned.

Which Virtue?

Which virtue did a person in this week’s lessons show most clearly?

Explain your choice in two or three sentences. Then name one place in your own life where this virtue will be asked of you.

Carry This Forward

The war debt, the Proclamation, the taxes, the soldiers, and the closing of Boston all pressed on rights the colonists believed they held. Peace was still possible until the king rejected the Olive Branch Petition. Remember that the Declaration argues in two steps: the principles first, and then the grievances as the proof.

British Policy to the Declaration

Part 1

From Victory to Quarrel

Chapter 1The Bill for a War
Chapter 2Taxes and Protest
Chapter 1

The Bill for a War

In 1763 Britain won the French and Indian War and took control of a huge stretch of North America. But the war had nearly doubled the nation’s debt. Parliament decided that the colonists, who had been defended, should help pay. At the same time, the king issued the Proclamation of 1763. It forbade colonists to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains, in order to keep the peace with Native nations and avoid new wars. But many colonists had fought for that land, and they felt cheated. Mountains and distance were now causing a quarrel.

Chapter 2

Taxes and Protest

Parliament then passed laws to raise money. The Sugar Act of 1764 put duties on goods brought into the colonies. The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed printed papers of every kind, such as newspapers, contracts, and even playing cards. It was the first tax placed directly on the colonists. They answered that only their own elected assemblies could tax them, since they had no members in Parliament. “No taxation without representation” became their cry. Merchants boycotted British goods, and crowds in the streets frightened the tax collectors.

The protest worked. In 1766 Parliament repealed the Stamp Act. But on the same day it passed the Declaratory Act, which said that Parliament could make laws for the colonies in all cases. Peace had returned, but the question underneath had not been answered. Who had the right to tax and govern the colonists?

In 1767 the Townshend Acts put new duties on glass, paper, paint, and tea. Colonists boycotted again. Britain sent soldiers to Boston to keep order. On March 5, 1770, a crowd taunted a group of soldiers, and the soldiers fired. Five colonists were killed in what was called the Boston Massacre. John Adams, a Boston lawyer who was no friend of mobs, defended the soldiers in court, and most were found not guilty. He believed that every man deserves a fair trial, even in an unpopular case.

Part 2

The Last Roads to Peace

Chapter 3Tea and Punishment
Chapter 4Shots and a Plea
Chapter 3

Tea and Punishment

In 1773 Parliament passed the Tea Act to help a struggling British company. The colonists saw it as another way to force a tax on them. In December, a group of men in Boston dumped hundreds of chests of tea into the harbor. Parliament answered in 1774 with laws the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. They closed Boston’s port until the tea was paid for, took away much of Massachusetts’s self-government, and again allowed the quartering of soldiers. Other colonies now saw that what had happened to Massachusetts could happen to them. They sent delegates to the First Continental Congress.

Chapter 4

Shots and a Plea

On April 19, 1775, British soldiers marched to Concord, Massachusetts, to seize military supplies. At Lexington and Concord, they met armed colonists, and the first shots of the war were fired. Even then, many delegates in the Second Continental Congress hoped that the quarrel might be settled. In July 1775 they sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III. The petition declared loyalty to the Crown and begged him to stop the fighting and to settle the dispute.

The king refused even to read it. Instead he declared that the colonies were in rebellion. Here was a road not taken. A king who listened might have kept the colonies. Reconciliation was still open until he closed it. Only after that did many colonists, such as those who read Paine’s Common Sense the next January, decide that independence was the only road left.

Part 3

Matching Grievances to Rights

Chapter 5The Declaration as a Charge Sheet
Chapter 5

The Declaration as a Charge Sheet

In June 1776 Congress named a committee of five to draft a declaration. Jefferson did most of the writing, with help from Adams, Franklin, and others. Congress voted for independence on July 2 and approved the final words on July 4. After the famous opening paragraphs, the Declaration lists many grievances against King George. Think of the list as a charge sheet. Each charge says: the king did this, and it violated a right.

Match a few. The Declaration says the king imposed “Taxes on us without our Consent.” That violates the right to property and the principle of consent of the governed. It says he deprived colonists “in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury.” That touches the right to liberty and a fair trial. It says he kept “Standing Armies among us, in times of peace, without the Consent of our legislatures,” and quartered large bodies of troops among them. That threatens both liberty and the safety of homes. It says he dissolved colonial assemblies, which attacks the right of people to govern themselves through representatives.

Now you can see why the Declaration is more than an angry letter. It does not say only that the colonists dislike British rule. It argues, one charge at a time, that the king broke the contract that made his rule just. If the charges are true, then Locke’s right of revolution applies. That is why its opening paragraphs on natural rights come first. The rest of the document is the proof.

A good citizen should be able to judge such an argument. Ask of each charge whether it is true and whether it is serious enough to justify so grave a step. That is the question you will take up in this lesson’s discussion. The Declaration asks the reader to decide, as it asked “a candid world.”
